drills.q: A CloudWatch bill jumps from $200 to $3,000/month right after a team adds 'more detailed per-user metrics.' Diagnose the mechanism precisely.
drills.a: A new metric dimension carrying high-cardinality values (e.g. userId) turns one logical metric into one billable metric PER distinct dimension value, since CloudWatch bills per unique combination of metric name, namespace, and dimension values. 10,000 distinct userIds on one metric name is 10,000 separate billable metrics at $0.30/month each in the first tier -- roughly $3,000/month, matching the described jump.

drills.q: Why does 'the first copy of CloudTrail management events per region is free' not guarantee a team pays nothing for CloudTrail?
drills.a: The free tier applies to the first trail's management events per region -- an overlapping second trail (e.g. an existing single-region trail plus a newly added multi-region trail both covering the same region) means the second copy of those same events is billed, unrelated to whether data events are ever touched. This is the '2nd-copy trap,' purely a trail-configuration issue.

drills.q: A team needs per-user debugging visibility but can't afford per-user CloudWatch metrics. What's the alternative architecture?
drills.a: Emit per-user detail as structured logs (JSON, optionally via Embedded Metric Format) instead of publishing per-user CloudWatch metrics. Query the per-user detail on demand via CloudWatch Logs Insights when actually debugging, rather than paying for a permanently-billed time series per user regardless of whether anyone looks at it. Keep the actual CloudWatch metrics aggregated to low-cardinality dimensions like route or status class.

drills.q: Would you recommend instrumenting a brand-new microservice directly against the X-Ray SDK in 2026? Why or why not, and what's the alternative?
drills.a: No -- the X-Ray SDK and daemon entered maintenance mode in February 2026, with AWS explicitly steering new instrumentation toward OpenTelemetry. OpenTelemetry can still export traces to X-Ray as a backend (or to any other OTel-compatible system), giving the same tracing capability with more vendor flexibility and avoiding a foreseeable future migration off a component that isn't receiving further investment.

drills.q: A compliance team asks for 'full audit logging on all S3 access across the account.' What's the risk of implementing this literally, and how do you scope it responsibly?
drills.a: Enabling S3 data events account-wide with no per-bucket scoping, at any meaningful access volume (an active data lake or ML pipeline can see millions of GET/PUT calls daily), can produce a CloudTrail bill that dwarfs the rest of the observability stack, since data events are billed at $0.10/100,000 from the very first event with no free tier. Responsible scoping: clarify whether the actual requirement covers every bucket or a defined sensitive-data scope, and use advanced event selectors to limit data-event logging to the specific buckets/prefixes that genuinely need it, rather than enabling it broadly by default.

drills.q: A Well-Architected review six months ago produced a long list of findings, and nothing on it has been fixed. What went wrong structurally, and how do you fix the process, not just the findings?
drills.a: The review was almost certainly treated as a one-time compliance exercise rather than a tracked backlog -- findings without prioritization (against AWS's own High-Risk Issue flag and actual blast radius) and without assigned owners and deadlines are functionally equivalent to not having done the review. Fix: re-run the review, prioritize findings explicitly, assign owners, and schedule a recurring re-review cadence so the framework functions as an ongoing discipline rather than a point-in-time audit.

drills.q: Why is 'idle provisioned capacity' (an oversized SageMaker endpoint or Redshift cluster) one of the hardest cost problems to catch with automated tooling like Cost Anomaly Detection?
drills.a: Cost Anomaly Detection is tuned to flag deviations from a resource's OWN historical spend baseline. A SageMaker endpoint or Redshift cluster provisioned for peak and simply always running at that size doesn't deviate from its own history -- it looks like steady, expected spend, not an anomaly. Catching it requires a separate utilization-based review comparing provisioned capacity against actual usage patterns, which is a different kind of check than anomaly detection provides.

drills.q: Your CFO gives you limited engineering time this quarter and asks for the single highest-leverage cost-observability improvement. What do you recommend and why not one of the specific point fixes (NAT, CloudTrail scoping, Athena partitioning)?
drills.a: Enforce cost allocation tagging at resource creation (via tag policies/SCPs) and enable Cost Anomaly Detection scoped to those tag groups. Tagging is the structural prerequisite for almost every other cost-visibility tool -- Cost Explorer filtering, Budgets scoping, and anomaly-detection granularity all depend on it, and untagged historical spend can never be retroactively attributed. The specific point fixes are real and worth doing, but they address symptoms already found; tagging makes every FUTURE anomaly (including ones not yet discovered) attributable and actionable quickly, which compounds in value in a way a one-time point fix does not.

drills.q: Explain why a finding like 'no autoscaling, capacity provisioned for peak' can legitimately appear under both the performance-efficiency and cost-optimization pillars of a Well-Architected review, and what that implies for prioritization.
drills.a: It violates the 'stop guessing capacity' cross-pillar design principle -- provisioning for an assumed worst case rather than autoscaling to real usage is simultaneously a performance-efficiency concern (capacity mismatch under variable load) and a cost-optimization concern (idle provisioned capacity is one of the top line items dominating real AI/data bills). A finding with cross-pillar impact should generally be weighted higher in remediation priority than an isolated single-pillar finding, since fixing it resolves two review findings at once and the pillars aren't independent silos.

drills.q: What's the Logs Insights cost-optimization lever, and how is it similar to and different from Athena's partitioning story?
drills.a: Logs Insights bills by volume of log data scanned per query, similar in shape to Athena's per-TB-scanned model, so the primary lever is scoping queries tightly by time range and log group rather than running broad, unscoped queries. It's different from Athena's story in that structuring log content as JSON improves query precision but does NOT reduce the bytes-scanned billing the way Parquet's columnar format reduces what Athena scans -- Logs Insights has no equivalent to 'read only the referenced columns.' The primary lever here is query scoping, not data format.
